content: During a caesarean section, the position of the mother can vary, with operating tables being tilted laterally, upwards, downwards, or flexed, and the use of wedges or cushions. However, there is currently no consensus on the optimal maternal positioning during this procedure. To investigate this, researchers reviewed all available data to determine if a specific maternal position during caesarean section could improve outcomes for both the mother and the neonate. They conducted a systematic search of databases, including the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register and PubMed, as well as manually reviewing references from relevant articles. The review included randomized trials comparing different maternal positions during caesarean sections. A total of 22 studies involving 857 women were identified, of which 11 studies were included in the analysis, while the other 11 were excluded. The included studies were of variable quality and often had small sample sizes. Most comparisons were based on data from single trials, which limits the reliability and applicability of the findings. The incidence of air embolism was not significantly different when comparing a head-up position to a horizontal position (average risk ratio [RR] 0.85; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.28 to 2.57). Similarly, there was no significant change in the occurrence of hypotensive episodes when comparing left lateral tilt (RR 0.11; 95% CI 0.01 to 1.94), right lateral tilt (RR 1.25; 95% CI 0.39 to 3.99), a right lumbar pelvic wedge (RR 0.85; 95% CI 0.53 to 1.37), or head-down tilt (RR 1.07; 95% CI 0.81 to 1.42) with horizontal positions. Additionally, no significant difference in hypotensive episodes was observed when comparing full lateral tilt with a 15-degree tilt (RR 1.20; 95% CI 0.80 to 1.79). However, the use of manual displacers was associated with a reduction in hypotensive episodes (RR 0.11; 95% CI 0.03 to 0.45). In contrast, hypotensive episodes were more frequent with a right lumbar wedge compared to a right pelvic wedge (RR 1.64; 95% CI 1.07 to 2.53) and with a right lateral tilt compared to a left lateral tilt (RR 3.30; 95% CI 1.20 to 9.08). Systolic blood pressure was not significantly affected when comparing left lateral tilt (mean difference [MD] 2.70; 95% CI -1.47 to 6.87) or head-down tilt (MD -3.00; 95% CI -8.38 to 2.38) with horizontal positions, or when comparing full lateral tilt with a 15-degree tilt (MD -5.00; 95% CI -11.45 to 1.45). However, manual displacers were associated with a smaller decrease in mean systolic blood pressure compared to left lateral tilt (MD -8.80; 95% CI -13.08 to -4.52). Diastolic blood pressure was not significantly affected when comparing left lateral tilt with horizontal positions (MD -1.90; 95% CI -5.28 to 1.48). However, diastolic pressure was lower in the head-down tilt position compared to horizontal positions (MD -7.00; 95% CI -12.05 to -1.95). There were no statistically significant differences in maternal pulse rate, five-minute Apgar scores, maternal blood pH, or cord blood pH when comparing different maternal positions during caesarean section. In conclusion, the evidence is limited and does not strongly support or refute the use of specific maternal positions, such as tilting or flexing the table, using wedges or cushions, or employing mechanical displacers. A left lateral tilt may be preferable to a right lateral tilt, and manual displacers may be more effective than a left lateral tilt in reducing hypotensive episodes. However, larger, high-quality studies are needed to confirm these findings and provide more definitive recommendations.
